systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : UNITED24 Media
Rubrique : Sanctions et export
Date du flux : 23/11/2026
Auteur : Cyril Barabaltchouk
Titre d'origine : EU Targets 60 Russian Banks, Shadow Fleet and Ex-Combatants in New Sanctions Package

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (UNITED24 Media) :
The European Commission proposed a 22nd sanctions package against Russia targeting banks, cryptocurrency networks, energy services, the shadow fleet, Russian former combatants, and entities supporting Moscow’s military industry, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on November 23.
The package focuses on four areas: Russia’s financing, energy sector, participation in European sporting and cultural events, and visa restrictions.
In the financial sector, the Commission proposed expanding restrictions on around 60 Russian banks, including cutting them off from the SWIFT international financial messaging system.
Brussels also plans to strengthen measures against cryptocurrency networks used to finance Russia and circumvent sanctions, with a dedicated cryptocurrency sanctions task force established for that work.
“We will focus on Russia, but we will also add third countries that help it circumvent our sanctions,” von der Leyen stated.
She added that combating sanctions circumvention would be a major element of the package and an area where the EU intends to coordinate with international partners.
The Commission also proposed expanding restrictions on energy-related services to prevent European companies from helping Russia build, operate, or repair energy infrastructure, including oil refineries.
For the first time, the proposed restrictions would also cover services connected to Russia’s electricity sector.
More than 70 additional vessels would be added to the EU sanctions list targeting Russia’s shadow fleet. The Commission also proposed banning tanker vessels insured in Russia.
Another part of the package would prohibit Russian former combatants from entering the European Union.
“We have recently witnessed an escalation of unconventional kinetic operations by Russian operatives in Europe,” von der Leyen stated.
“Former Russian combatants pose a security threat to Europe. They cannot be allowed to move freely across our countries. Therefore, they will be banned from entering the European Union.”
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also announced proposed measures targeting the Russian and Belarusian military-industrial sectors.
More than 100 additional entries would be added to the sanctions list, including companies involved in circumventing EU restrictions. Export controls would also be tightened against more than 20 entities, while additional goods that could contribute to Russia’s war against Ukraine would face export restrictions.
Restrictions on Russian former combatants had already been under discussion before the package was unveiled. On November 16, Kallas confirmed that the EU was considering a bloc-wide entry ban for Russians who participated in the full-scale invasion, although some member states still had questions about its implementation.

SOURCE 2 (INSIGHT EU MONITORING) :
Brussels, 23 November 2026
Today, alongside the proposal for the EU’s 22nd sanctions package, the Commission is taking action to strengthen Europe’s security, ensuring that those linked to Russia’s war of aggression are banned from our territory and cannot become a security risk or the Union and its citizens.
The Commission has today adopted revised guidelines to support the implementation of the visa ban on current and former combatants, as set out in the 21st sanctions package and today’s proposal for the 22nd sanctions package.
The revised guidelines are accompanied by an updated list of supporting documents for Russian visa applicants. They also include stricter measures on tourist visas and on individual artists traveling to the EU as well as guidance on how to implement the proposed ban for Russian athletes from competing on behalf of Russia at sport events in the EU. Together, these measures underline the EU’s determination to apply sustained political pressure on Russia and those connected to its aggression and do not accept a return to business as usual until a just and lasting peace for Ukraine is achieved.
Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said: “We have proposed to activate an EU visa ban for anyone who is serving or has served in Russia’s Armed forces since the beginning of its war of aggression. As we see a rise in non-conventional kinetic activities of Russian operatives across Member States, this ban is part of our response. Entry to the European Union must be off limits for those that pose a security risk to Europe”.
Visa ban on ex and current Russian combatants
Following the 21st sanctions package, the Commission and the High Representative have today put forward the necessary initiatives to propose the activation of the EU visa ban for anyone who is serving or has served in the Russian Armed Forces since the beginning of Russia’s war of aggression. With today’s guidelines and supporting documents, Member States will have the tools necessary to put this ban in practice.
- Enhanced checks should focus on individuals who are serving or have served in Russian armed forces or associated armed groups since 24 February 2022 and directly participated in combat operations in Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Combatants of the Russian Armed Forces of other nationalities are also subject to the visa ban because they represent an equal threat to EU security.
- The updated list of supporting documents provides additional elements for national authorities to identify Russian combatants – such as a questionnaire regarding military service, a self-declaration, and the possibility to request documents, such as a military booklet.
Stricter rules for non-essential travel
- Russian nationals continue to pose high security risks for the European Union, including hybrid threats, disinformation, acts of sabotage and espionage, and other hostile activities. Therefore, the updated guidelines recommend a very strict approach to issuing tourist visas for Russians. Member States should no longer recognise non-biometric Russian passports given high fraud and security risks.
- Stronger checks at EU external borders should be conducted by border guards with thorough individual assessments of all Russian nationals seeking to enter the Schengen area, regardless of where they have travelled from.
- Checks should include interviews and systematic fingerprint checks in the Schengen Information System (SIS). Member States are encouraged to enter SIS alerts following individual decisions to refuse entry on public policy or internal security grounds, to prevent entry from entering through another border crossing.
New measures on Russian athletes and individual artists
Today’s updated guidelines also align with today’s proposal for the 22nd package for a ban on Russian nationals to compete on behalf of the Russian state at sporting events in the EU. When that ban is adopted, Member States notably should consider refusing Schengen visas to Russian athletes competing in sporting events where Russian national symbols such as the flag, anthem, or uniforms are used.
The guidelines call as well for specific attention to be given to individual artists participating in cultural events, who are sponsored by the Russian authorities and who can use their visibility in favour of Russia’s war of aggression.
Next steps
The Commission will work with Member States to support consistent and harmonised implementation of the guidelines and the revised list of supporting documents.
Following the adoption by the Commission of the revised guidelines and the list of supporting documents, the High Representative has put forward the proposal to start applying the visa ban on Russian combatants concerning restrictive measures towards Russia. The Council will then decide when the visa ban on Russian combatants enters into force across the EU.
Background
In 2022, the EU fully suspended the visa facilitation agreement with Russia. Since 2022, the Commission adopted additional measures to stop facilitating visa issuance for Russian nationals. This led to reducing visa issuance. The measures adopted today will further support Member States in their visa application assessment at consulates and at the EU’s external borders in identifying the persons concerned and applying the relevant restrictions. The Commission continues to monitor their implementation and work with Member States to ensure consistent application.
The EU maintains safeguards for those needing protection. Enhanced scrutiny must not prevent entry by people with a legitimate interest in leaving Russia, notably human rights defenders, dissidents and independent journalists. Humanitarian exceptions should also be considered for Ukrainians who were forcibly granted Russian nationality and can prove their previous Ukrainian citizenship.
For more information
The documents corresponding to this communication will be available later. The press release will be updated then, including the links to the documents, once they are available.

Statement by President von der Leyen on the 22nd package of sanctions against Russia
Strasbourg, 23 November 2026
Good afternoon,
Today, we present our 22nd package of sanctions. The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine. And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine. With this package, we are increasing the pressure in three ways. We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war by targeting its banks and crypto platforms. We are further isolating Russia. We are shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events. We are tightening our visa rules. And we are doubling down on enforcement.
Allow me to go into some of the key elements. First, on financial services. We are extending the transaction ban to some 60 Russian banks. All 60 banks will be removed from the SWIFT system. And we are cracking down on the crypto and payment networks. We will focus on Russia but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions. This is a major focus of our new package. And an important area where we want to align efforts with international partners. This is the reason why we have also launched a Crypto Sanctions Task Force to support this work.
Second, on the Russian energy sector. We are expanding the energy services ban so that no European company can help Russia build, operate or repair its energy infrastructures, and notably its refineries. For the first time, this ban also covers electricity services. On the Russian Shadow Fleet, we are listing over 70 more ships. And we are proposing to ban all tanker vessels which are insured in Russia.
Third, we have proposed a visa ban for Russian ex-combatants. We have recently seen an escalation in non-conventional kinetic activities of Russian operatives in Europe. And this ban is a part of our response. Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries. Therefore, entry into the European Union will be off limits.
Fourth, we will prohibit Europeans from continuing to occupy posts in the governing bodies of companies in Russia. There cannot be business as usual in our economic relations with Russia.
And finally, on sports and culture. Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities. Today, for any sports events in the EU, we are introducing bans on Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag. We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European-based sports and cultural associations. And we will introduce restrictions on Russians holding posts in governing bodies of European based sports federations.
Our position is clear: we are giving Ukraine the strength to secure peace – and Russia every reason to choose it.
Source – EU Commission
